images.title: Two squares land on one face
images.purpose: Show why six squares can fail to fold into a cube: two squares land on the same face.
images.composition: One arrangement of six squares centred on white, with the two squares that collide highlighted.
images.exact_structure: Six equal squares, each about 15 percent of the frame height, with thin dark outlines, centred: a horizontal row of 4 squares numbered '1', '2', '3', '4' from left to right; one square directly above square 1, labelled 'lid'; and one more square directly to the left of the lid square (above and left of square 1). Squares 1, 2, 3 and the lid are white. Square 4 and the leftmost square are both filled reddish purple #CC79A7, and one thin curved #CC79A7 arrow runs from the leftmost square over to square 4, labelled 'same face'. Under the row, in vermilion #D55E00, 'not a net'.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: If two squares fold onto the same face, the shape is not a net of a cube.
images.description: Show why six squares can fail to fold into a cube: two squares land on the same face.
images.context: One clean concept image for T7.C2.
images.teaching_notes: Row folds into four walls with 1 at the front and 4 on the left; the square left of the lid folds onto wall 4 and the bottom stays open.

image_decisions.why: The overlap is the whole test; seeing which two squares collide makes it clear.
